evidence: Cic. Leg. 1.55: quod decus antīquī summum bonum esse dīxērunt (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: What belongs to a time long past, the opposite of novus; as a noun, antīquī are the ancients, above all the old writers. It can also mean simply former, earlier, and its comparative, more important: quod honestius, id mihi est antīquius (Cic. Att. 7.3, Lewis & Short). For a worn object say vetus (see old).

terms.gloss: old, of long standing; as a noun, the men of old
evidence: Cic. Univ. 11: crēdendum est veteribus et prīscīs virīs (Lewis & Short, s.v. prīscus)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short sets the two apart: vetus is what has existed a long time (the opposite of recēns), antīquus what belongs to a time that is past. Veterēs, too, are the ancients.

evidence: Hor. Epod. 2.2: ut prīsca gēns mortālium
terms.comment: What was there before our time, with a sense of venerable age; from Augustus on, what dates from the earliest days of Rome (Lewis & Short). Lewis & Short leaves the i unmarked; de Vaan prints prīscus, and the loci write prīsca.

phrases.latin: tum coquus, vīlissimum antīquīs mancipium et aestimātiōne et ūsū, in pretiō esse, et quod ministerium fuerat, ars habērī coepta
phrases.english: then the cook, to the ancients the cheapest of slaves both in value and in use, began to be prized, and what had been a chore came to be thought an art
(the river Limia,) called the river of Forgetfulness by the ancients, and the stuff of many tales

phrases.latin: prīsca juvent aliōs: ego mē nunc dēnique nātum grātulor: haec aetās mōribus apta meīs
phrases.english: let the old days please others: I am glad I was born now; this age suits my ways

phrases.latin: sērō tē amāvī, pulchritūdō tam antīqua et tam nova
phrases.english: late have I loved you, beauty so ancient and so new
